transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I guess the main thing that pushed me to come in is… I’m having trouble really taking in what people say, even when I’m trying to listen. Like my wife will be talking to me about my cousin’s appointments or who’s giving him a ride and when, and I’ll be looking right at her, nodding along like I’m following, but then a minute later I realize I only caught pieces of it. Half of what she said is just kind of gone.

It’s not that I don’t care, because I do, and I’m usually making an effort. But she’ll ask, “Did you hear me?” and I’ll think, well, I was hearing words, but I didn’t actually absorb it. That’s been frustrating and a little embarrassing, honestly, and it’s happening enough that I figured I should talk to someone about it.
Is this trouble with taking in what people say happening all the time, or does it come and go?

It kind of comes and goes, I guess, but it happens often enough that it feels like a real pattern now. It’s not every single conversation, or at least I don’t notice it every single time. But the thing that really made me come in is with my wife—she’ll be telling me something practical, like about my cousin’s appointments or who’s supposed to give him a ride and when, and I’m sitting there looking right at her, nodding, thinking I’m listening.

Then a minute later I realize I only took in bits and pieces. Like I heard her voice, I know she was talking, but I didn’t actually hold onto half of what she said. It’s embarrassing because from the outside I probably look like I’m paying attention, and I’m not trying to ignore her. So… not constant every second, but it happens enough that it’s become a problem.
Do you notice this happening more often when you're stressed or anxious?

Maybe a little, but honestly I notice it even when I’m not especially worked up. The example that really stands out is still with my wife, when she’s telling me about my cousin’s appointments or rides—like who’s taking him where, what time something is, that kind of thing.

I’ll be looking right at her, and I’m not off doing something else in my mind on purpose. I’m nodding, I’m trying to follow along, and in the moment I feel like I’m listening. But then a minute later, when I try to repeat it back or she asks me something about it, I realize I only kept maybe part of it. Like half of what she said just didn’t really land.

So I wouldn’t say it’s only when I’m stressed or anxious. Stress might make it worse, I guess, but the frustrating part is it can happen during a normal conversation where I should be able to take it in.
Do you feel like your mood or emotional state affects how well you can focus on and remember conversations?

I don’t know that I can pin it directly on my mood, exactly. I mean, if I’m upset or distracted emotionally, I’m sure that doesn’t help, but the part that bothers me is it happens even when I feel pretty normal.

Like the example I keep coming back to is my wife talking to me about my cousin’s appointments or rides—who’s supposed to take him, what time, that kind of thing. I’ll be looking right at her, not angry, not especially anxious, just sitting there trying to listen. And I’ll even nod along because I think I’m following her. But then a minute later, it’s like I realize I didn’t actually take in half of what she said.

So maybe my emotional state can make it worse sometimes, but I don’t think it explains it all. It’s more like my attention just doesn’t hold onto the conversation the way it should, even when I care about what she’s saying.
Do you have trouble with learning new things or solving problems in your daily life?

I’m not sure I’d say I have a major problem with learning new things or solving problems, at least not in a clear-cut way. I mean, it depends what you mean by learning, I guess.

If it’s something totally new and there are a lot of steps or details, I can feel a little slower getting it all straight in my head. Like I may need someone to explain it again, or I might have to write it down and go back over it, otherwise pieces of it don’t really stick. But I don’t know if that’s “learning trouble” exactly, or just me needing more time and repetition than I used to.

With solving problems day to day, I usually can figure things out eventually. I don’t feel like I’m unable to reason things through. It’s more that if there are too many moving parts, I can get kind of bogged down and have to slow it way down. But I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed some big, obvious inability to learn or solve problems. It’s more… I’m not totally sure how to separate that from just getting distracted or losing track of details.
Do you have trouble remembering things that didn't involve conversations, like where you placed items or what you did yesterday?

Yeah, that happens too. The main thing I notice is misplacing stuff around the house. I’ll put my keys down somewhere, or my phone, and then ten minutes later I’m walking around trying to reconstruct where I was—kitchen, living room, by the door, back to the kitchen—because I have no idea where I set it.

And it’s not always just the usual keys-and-phone thing. I’ve done it with catering receipts too, where I know I had them in my hand and then somehow they end up on a counter or under some papers. Or I’ll be out in the yard with the garden clippers, set them down “just for a second,” and then I’m wandering around looking in three different places because I can’t remember where that second was.

It’s not like I forget my whole day yesterday, exactly. It’s more these little practical things—where did I put that, what was I just doing with it—and then I lose time retracing my steps. It’s frustrating because it feels like I should be able to remember something I did two minutes ago.
Have you noticed any impact on your relationships or work because of these difficulties with paying attention and remembering things?

Yeah, it has, mostly at home. I wouldn’t say everything is falling apart or anything like that, but there’s definitely more tension than there used to be.

The biggest thing is with my wife and my cousin’s care. She’ll tell me something about an appointment, or who’s supposed to take him, or some detail that needs to be handled, and then later I’ll either have to ask her again or I’ll get mixed up about what she said. And I can tell it frustrates her, because from her side it probably feels like, “I already told you this, why didn’t you listen?” Or like she can’t really count on me to hold onto the details. I don’t like that, because I do care, and I’m not trying to dump it back on her. But I can see why she gets irritated.

And with work-type stuff, well, I’m not working a regular job now, but with catering tasks or small things I help with, I’ve had to double-check myself more. Like making sure I didn’t mix up a receipt, or forget one part of a small task, or put something in the wrong place. Sometimes I’ll redo something just because I’m not confident I got it right the first time. It’s not huge disasters, but it slows things down and makes me feel like I can’t just trust my own first pass at things.
Have you been experiencing any headaches, fatigue, or other physical symptoms lately?

Not really in any clear way, no. I mean, I get the normal tiredness you’d expect sometimes, but I haven’t been noticing headaches or some new physical thing that stands out to me. Nothing where I’d say, “Oh, this is a symptom I need to tell the doctor about,” if that makes sense.

I guess I’m not always great at tracking little things unless they’re really obvious, but as far as headaches, fatigue, or other physical symptoms lately, nothing specific is coming to mind.
Do you ever feel mentally foggy or confused, even when you're not trying to focus on a specific conversation or task?

I’m not sure I’d call it confused, exactly. Like, I don’t usually sit there and feel like I don’t know where I am or what’s going on. It’s more that my mind can feel kind of… not fully lined up, if that makes sense.

But even then, I don’t know if I’d describe that as foggy. I think of foggy as almost like being sick or really sleep-deprived, where everything feels dulled down, and I can’t say I’ve noticed that in a clear way. A lot of the time I feel basically normal until there’s something I’m supposed to keep track of, and then I realize I’ve drifted or lost the thread.

If I’m just sitting around not trying to focus on anything specific, I don’t think I’m generally confused. Maybe I get a little mentally scattered sometimes, but not confused like I’m disoriented or anything.
Do you find that you have trouble paying attention or remembering things in situations other than conversations with your wife?

Yes, definitely. It’s not only with my wife, although that’s where it shows up the most because those conversations matter and she notices when I miss something.

But it happens in other situations too. Like if I sit down to work out a catering order, I’ll start off fine — I’m looking at the list, the numbers, what needs to go where — and then after a little while I realize my mind has wandered. Not even to anything important, sometimes just some random thought, and then I look back at the paper or the notes and it’s like, wait, did I already account for this? Did I read that correctly? So I end up going back over the same thing again, almost like I never really read it the first time.

It’s similar if I’m listening through a parish planning call. I can follow it at the beginning, and I’m trying to pay attention, but then somewhere in the middle I’ll lose the thread. Then someone mentions something later and I’m thinking, “Did we already decide that?” or “Was I supposed to remember who was handling that?” So I’ll check notes or try to piece it back together.

So yeah, it’s not just conversations with her. It’s more any situation where I have to keep attention going for a while and hold onto details. I can start okay, but staying with it is the hard part.
Do you find yourself losing interest in the things you're trying to pay attention to, which might be why you're having trouble remembering them?

Not exactly, no. I mean, sometimes the thing itself isn’t thrilling — like working through a catering order isn’t exactly exciting — but I don’t think it’s that I lose interest and then stop caring. I can still care about getting it right.

It’s more like I sit down and start off fine. I know what I’m supposed to be doing, I’m looking at the list or the notes, and I’m following it. Then after a little while, without really deciding to, my mind just wanders off. And when I come back to it, I’m not always sure what I actually took in. So I’ll have to go back over the same notes again, almost like I never read them the first time.

Same kind of thing with a parish planning call. I may be interested in what’s being discussed, or at least I know it matters, but somewhere in the middle I’ll realize I missed part of it. Then I’m trying to catch up from context or look back at notes. So I wouldn’t say it’s mostly losing interest. It feels more like I have trouble keeping my attention on it long enough, even when I’m trying to.
Did your trouble with paying attention and remembering things start after something significant happened in your life?

It did seem to get noticeably harder after my cousin moved in with us, yes. That was after his surgery, and he’s been staying with us, and I’d say that was about… maybe 11 months ago now.

I don’t know that it started from absolutely nowhere right then, like flipping a switch, but that’s when I really began noticing it more. Before that I might have had moments of drifting or needing to reread things, but since he moved in, it’s been harder to keep track of things and remember details the way I need to. So if you’re asking whether there was a life change around when it got worse, yes — that’s the main one that comes to mind.
Did you notice any significant change in your ability to pay attention and remember things immediately after your cousin moved in with you?

Not immediately like the next day, no — at least I don’t remember it as a sudden, sharp change right when he walked in the door, if that makes sense.

It was more that after he moved in with us after the surgery, over that stretch of time, I started noticing it was harder. And now looking back, it’s been about 11 months where paying attention and remembering details has felt noticeably more difficult than before. At first I probably brushed it off, like, “Well, there’s more going on in the house,” or “I’m just distracted today,” but it kept showing up enough that I began to recognize it as a real change.

So I’d say the timing lines up with him moving in, but not as an instant thing — more something that became clear over the months since then.
Do you have trouble with making decisions or planning tasks?

I’m not sure I’d call that the main problem, honestly. Planning tasks… I mean, I can usually figure out what needs to be done if I sit down and think it through. Decisions too — I don’t think I’m someone who just can’t decide anything.

Sometimes if there are a lot of pieces, I may need to slow down and write things out, because otherwise it feels a little muddled. But I don’t know if that’s trouble making decisions exactly, or just needing to organize myself better. Like, if someone asks me to choose between two straightforward things, I can usually do that.

So… not really, or at least I haven’t noticed it as much as the attention and remembering part.
Do you feel anything physically, like a sensation or a feeling in your body, when you realize your mind has wandered off?

I don’t think I feel anything physical, no. At least nothing that I’ve really noticed as a clear body sensation.

It’s more like I suddenly realize, “Oh, I wasn’t paying attention,” or I’ve lost the thread of what someone was saying. But I wouldn’t say I get, like, a feeling in my chest or stomach or anything like that. Maybe sometimes there’s a little frustration after I notice it, but that’s more my reaction to realizing I drifted off, not a physical warning sign or sensation beforehand.

So I guess the answer is no, not really — I mostly notice it mentally, after the fact.
Do you feel anything physically when you realize you've lost focus on a task?

Not that I can really identify, no. When I realize I’ve lost focus on a task, it’s usually more like I sort of “come to” mentally and notice I’ve been off track. Like I’ll look at what I was doing and think, “Wait, what was I just doing?” or “How did I get sidetracked from this?”

But physically, I don’t think there’s a specific feeling that goes with it. I don’t notice, you know, tension in my body or a stomach feeling or anything like that. If anything, there may be a little irritation with myself afterward, because I have to back up and figure out where I left off, but that feels more emotional than physical.

So I guess I’d say no, I haven’t noticed a body sensation when it happens.
Are you finding it harder to manage your daily responsibilities because of these attention and memory issues?

Yeah… I think it is starting to, at least in some ways. I wouldn’t say my whole day is falling apart or anything like that, but it’s causing problems where it matters.

At home especially, it’s become kind of a sore point with my wife. She feels like she can’t totally count on me with my cousin’s care, and I understand why she feels that way, even if it’s hard to hear. It’s not that I don’t care or I’m trying to avoid helping — I do want to be reliable — but if I forget something or don’t keep track of a detail, then she ends up feeling like she has to check behind me. And that creates tension between us.

And then with the catering tasks I still help with, I’ve noticed I have to double-check things more than I used to. Small jobs can get mixed up if I’m not careful, so I’ll go back over what I did or sometimes have to redo something just to make sure it’s right. It’s frustrating because these aren’t huge complicated things, but if I don’t slow down and check, little mistakes can happen.

So yes, I’d say it’s affecting daily responsibilities some. Maybe mildly, but enough that other people notice, and enough that it causes stress.
Are you finding it harder to maintain relationships or manage daily tasks because of these issues with attention and memory?

Yes, I think so. Not in a dramatic way, like everything is unmanageable, but it has definitely started to affect things.

The biggest thing is at home. It’s caused some tension with my wife because she feels like she can’t fully count on me when it comes to helping with my cousin’s care. And I understand why she feels that way, even if it makes me feel bad. If I forget a detail or don’t follow through the way I meant to, then she feels like she has to check behind me or keep track of things herself, and that wears on both of us. I don’t want her to feel like she has another thing to manage because of me.

And with the catering stuff I still help with, I’ve noticed I can’t just assume I did everything right the first time. I have to double-check things, sometimes go back and redo small tasks, because otherwise little jobs can get mixed up. It’s frustrating because they’re not huge, complicated things, but if my attention slips, it creates extra work.

So yeah, I’d say it’s making daily tasks harder, and relationship-wise it’s mainly that tension at home from not seeming as dependable as I want to be.
Are you feeling overwhelmed by the impact of these attention and memory issues on your daily life and relationships?

Overwhelmed might be a little strong, but… yeah, I do feel worn down by it sometimes. It’s not like I can’t function day to day, but it’s the way these little lapses keep showing up in places where people are depending on me.

At home, that’s probably where it bothers me the most. My wife has started feeling like she can’t fully count on me with my cousin’s care, and that’s hard, because I don’t want to add to her stress or make her feel like she has to supervise me. I can tell it creates tension, even if neither of us is trying to turn it into a fight. It’s more that she’ll be uncertain whether I remembered something or handled something the way I was supposed to, and then I feel bad because I know she has enough on her plate.

And with the catering tasks I still help with, I’ve had to be a lot more careful than I used to be. I’ll double-check things, or sometimes I’ll realize something small got mixed up and I have to redo it. It’s not a huge disaster, but it’s frustrating because these are small jobs, and I don’t like feeling like I can’t just trust myself to keep them straight the first time.

So I wouldn’t say I’m completely overwhelmed, but it does weigh on me. It’s enough that I’m noticing it, and other people are noticing it too.
Do you think your symptoms started after a particularly stressful event or period in your life?

I don’t know if I’d say it started after a stressful event exactly, like one big shock or something, but it did become noticeably harder around the time my cousin moved in with us after surgery.

That was about… maybe 11 months ago now. Before that, I’m sure I had moments where I’d forget things or get scattered, but it wasn’t standing out to me in the same way. Once he came to stay with us and there were more things to keep track of, more responsibility in the house, that’s when I really started noticing that I wasn’t keeping up as well as I thought I should.

So I guess the timing does line up with that period. I wouldn’t want to say the surgery or him moving in “caused” it, because I don’t really know that, but that’s when it became harder to ignore.

A lot of the time I feel basically normal until there’s something I’m supposed to keep track of, and then I realize I’ve drifted or lost the thread.

If I’m just sitting around not trying to focus on anything specific, I don’t think I’m generally confused. Maybe I get a little mentally scattered sometimes, but not confused like I’m disoriented or anything.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences difficulties with attention and memory consistently across different contexts and tasks
doctor.question: Do you find that you have trouble paying attention or remembering things in situations other than conversations with your wife?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: If I sit down to work out a catering order or listen through a parish planning call, I start off fine, but before long my mind wanders and I have to go back over the same notes like I never read them.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether attention problems happen outside direct conversations with my wife, such as during tasks or calls, which matches difficulty sustaining attention in other activities.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. It’s not only with my wife, although that’s where it shows up the most because those conversations matter and she notices when I miss something.

But it happens in other situations too. Like if I sit down to work out a catering order, I’ll start off fine — I’m looking at the list, the numbers, what needs to go where — and then after a little while I realize my mind has wandered. Not even to anything important, sometimes just some random thought, and then I look back at the paper or the notes and it’s like, wait, did I already account for this? Did I read that correctly? So I end up going back over the same thing again, almost like I never really read it the first time.

It’s similar if I’m listening through a parish planning call. I can follow it at the beginning, and I’m trying to pay attention, but then somewhere in the middle I’ll lose the thread. Then someone mentions something later and I’m thinking, “Did we already decide that?” or “Was I supposed to remember who was handling that?” So I’ll check notes or try to piece it back together.

So yeah, it’s not just conversations with her. It’s more any situation where I have to keep attention going for a while and hold onto details. I can start okay, but staying with it is the hard part.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with paying attention is related to a lack of interest
doctor.question: Do you find yourself losing interest in the things you're trying to pay attention to, which might be why you're having trouble remembering them?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: If I sit down to work out a catering order or listen through a parish planning call, I start off fine, but before long my mind wanders and I have to go back over the same notes like I never read them.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether difficulty maintaining attention on tasks leads to not remembering them, which most directly matches sustained attention difficulty.

patient.answer:
Not exactly, no. I mean, sometimes the thing itself isn’t thrilling — like working through a catering order isn’t exactly exciting — but I don’t think it’s that I lose interest and then stop caring. I can still care about getting it right.

It’s more like I sit down and start off fine. I know what I’m supposed to be doing, I’m looking at the list or the notes, and I’m following it. Then after a little while, without really deciding to, my mind just wanders off. And when I come back to it, I’m not always sure what I actually took in. So I’ll have to go back over the same notes again, almost like I never read them the first time.

Same kind of thing with a parish planning call. I may be interested in what’s being discussed, or at least I know it matters, but somewhere in the middle I’ll realize I missed part of it. Then I’m trying to catch up from context or look back at notes. So I wouldn’t say it’s mostly losing interest. It feels more like I have trouble keeping my attention on it long enough, even when I’m trying to.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with attention and memory is associated with a specific event or period in their life
doctor.question: Did your trouble with paying attention and remembering things start after something significant happened in your life?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been noticeably harder for about 11 months, since my cousin moved in with us after surgery.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the attention and memory problems began and whether they followed a significant life event; this matches the profile noting the symptoms became noticeably harder about 11 months ago after the cousin moved in after surgery.

patient.answer:
It did seem to get noticeably harder after my cousin moved in with us, yes. That was after his surgery, and he’s been staying with us, and I’d say that was about… maybe 11 months ago now.

I don’t know that it started from absolutely nowhere right then, like flipping a switch, but that’s when I really began noticing it more. Before that I might have had moments of drifting or needing to reread things, but since he moved in, it’s been harder to keep track of things and remember details the way I need to. So if you’re asking whether there was a life change around when it got worse, yes — that’s the main one that comes to mind.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's symptoms are related to a specific stressful event
doctor.question: Did you notice any significant change in your ability to pay attention and remember things immediately after your cousin moved in with you?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been noticeably harder for about 11 months, since my cousin moved in with us after surgery.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about the timing of when the attention and memory problems changed, specifically after the cousin moved in, which matches the duration item.

patient.answer:
Not immediately like the next day, no — at least I don’t remember it as a sudden, sharp change right when he walked in the door, if that makes sense.

It was more that after he moved in with us after the surgery, over that stretch of time, I started noticing it was harder. And now looking back, it’s been about 11 months where paying attention and remembering details has felt noticeably more difficult than before. At first I probably brushed it off, like, “Well, there’s more going on in the house,” or “I’m just distracted today,” but it kept showing up enough that I began to recognize it as a real change.

So I’d say the timing lines up with him moving in, but not as an instant thing — more something that became clear over the months since then.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any other cognitive difficulties besides attention and memory
doctor.question: Do you have trouble with making decisions or planning tasks?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about difficulty making decisions or planning tasks, which is not directly covered by the provided symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d call that the main problem, honestly. Planning tasks… I mean, I can usually figure out what needs to be done if I sit down and think it through. Decisions too — I don’t think I’m someone who just can’t decide anything.

Sometimes if there are a lot of pieces, I may need to slow down and write things out, because otherwise it feels a little muddled. But I don’t know if that’s trouble making decisions exactly, or just needing to organize myself better. Like, if someone asks me to choose between two straightforward things, I can usually do that.

So… not really, or at least I haven’t noticed it as much as the attention and remembering part.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any physical symptoms when their attention wanders
doctor.question: Do you feel anything physically, like a sensation or a feeling in your body, when you realize your mind has wandered off?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical sensations in the body when noticing mind-wandering, but the symptom profile does not include bodily sensations or somatic experiences.

patient.answer:
I don’t think I feel anything physical, no. At least nothing that I’ve really noticed as a clear body sensation.

It’s more like I suddenly realize, “Oh, I wasn’t paying attention,” or I’ve lost the thread of what someone was saying. But I wouldn’t say I get, like, a feeling in my chest or stomach or anything like that. Maybe sometimes there’s a little frustration after I notice it, but that’s more my reaction to realizing I drifted off, not a physical warning sign or sensation beforehand.

So I guess the answer is no, not really — I mostly notice it mentally, after the fact.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any physical symptoms when their mind wanders off during tasks
doctor.question: Do you feel anything physically when you realize you've lost focus on a task?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about physical sensations when noticing lost focus, and the symptom profile does not include physical feelings or bodily sensations associated with inattention.

patient.answer:
Not that I can really identify, no. When I realize I’ve lost focus on a task, it’s usually more like I sort of “come to” mentally and notice I’ve been off track. Like I’ll look at what I was doing and think, “Wait, what was I just doing?” or “How did I get sidetracked from this?”

But physically, I don’t think there’s a specific feeling that goes with it. I don’t notice, you know, tension in my body or a stomach feeling or anything like that. If anything, there may be a little irritation with myself afterward, because I have to back up and figure out where I left off, but that feels more emotional than physical.

So I guess I’d say no, I haven’t noticed a body sensation when it happens.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting daily life
doctor.question: Are you finding it harder to manage your daily responsibilities because of these attention and memory issues?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started causing tension at home because my wife feels she can’t count on me with my cousin’s care, and I’ve had to double-check or redo catering tasks so small jobs don’t get mixed up.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the attention and memory issues are making daily responsibilities harder to manage, which directly concerns impairment in functioning.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I think it is starting to, at least in some ways. I wouldn’t say my whole day is falling apart or anything like that, but it’s causing problems where it matters.

At home especially, it’s become kind of a sore point with my wife. She feels like she can’t totally count on me with my cousin’s care, and I understand why she feels that way, even if it’s hard to hear. It’s not that I don’t care or I’m trying to avoid helping — I do want to be reliable — but if I forget something or don’t keep track of a detail, then she ends up feeling like she has to check behind me. And that creates tension between us.

And then with the catering tasks I still help with, I’ve noticed I have to double-check things more than I used to. Small jobs can get mixed up if I’m not careful, so I’ll go back over what I did or sometimes have to redo something just to make sure it’s right. It’s frustrating because these aren’t huge complicated things, but if I don’t slow down and check, little mistakes can happen.

So yes, I’d say it’s affecting daily responsibilities some. Maybe mildly, but enough that other people notice, and enough that it causes stress.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Are you finding it harder to maintain relationships or manage daily tasks because of these issues with attention and memory?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started causing tension at home because my wife feels she can’t count on me with my cousin’s care, and I’ve had to double-check or redo catering tasks so small jobs don’t get mixed up.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether attention and memory issues are causing problems in relationships or daily task management, which directly concerns functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think so. Not in a dramatic way, like everything is unmanageable, but it has definitely started to affect things.

The biggest thing is at home. It’s caused some tension with my wife because she feels like she can’t fully count on me when it comes to helping with my cousin’s care. And I understand why she feels that way, even if it makes me feel bad. If I forget a detail or don’t follow through the way I meant to, then she feels like she has to check behind me or keep track of things herself, and that wears on both of us. I don’t want her to feel like she has another thing to manage because of me.

And with the catering stuff I still help with, I’ve noticed I can’t just assume I did everything right the first time. I have to double-check things, sometimes go back and redo small tasks, because otherwise little jobs can get mixed up. It’s frustrating because they’re not huge, complicated things, but if my attention slips, it creates extra work.

So yeah, I’d say it’s making daily tasks harder, and relationship-wise it’s mainly that tension at home from not seeming as dependable as I want to be.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are significantly impacting their daily life and relationships
doctor.question: Are you feeling overwhelmed by the impact of these attention and memory issues on your daily life and relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: It has started causing tension at home because my wife feels she can’t count on me with my cousin’s care, and I’ve had to double-check or redo catering tasks so small jobs don’t get mixed up.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about how the attention and memory issues are affecting daily life and relationships, which most directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Overwhelmed might be a little strong, but… yeah, I do feel worn down by it sometimes. It’s not like I can’t function day to day, but it’s the way these little lapses keep showing up in places where people are depending on me.

At home, that’s probably where it bothers me the most. My wife has started feeling like she can’t fully count on me with my cousin’s care, and that’s hard, because I don’t want to add to her stress or make her feel like she has to supervise me. I can tell it creates tension, even if neither of us is trying to turn it into a fight. It’s more that she’ll be uncertain whether I remembered something or handled something the way I was supposed to, and then I feel bad because I know she has enough on her plate.

And with the catering tasks I still help with, I’ve had to be a lot more careful than I used to be. I’ll double-check things, or sometimes I’ll realize something small got mixed up and I have to redo it. It’s not a huge disaster, but it’s frustrating because these are small jobs, and I don’t like feeling like I can’t just trust myself to keep them straight the first time.

So I wouldn’t say I’m completely overwhelmed, but it does weigh on me. It’s enough that I’m noticing it, and other people are noticing it too.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are consistent with a specific disorder
doctor.question: Do you think your symptoms started after a particularly stressful event or period in your life?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been noticeably harder for about 11 months, since my cousin moved in with us after surgery.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about timing and whether the symptoms became noticeable after a stressful life period; this profile notes they have been noticeably harder for about 11 months, since the cousin moved in after surgery.

patient.answer:
I don’t know if I’d say it started after a stressful event exactly, like one big shock or something, but it did become noticeably harder around the time my cousin moved in with us after surgery.

That was about… maybe 11 months ago now. Before that, I’m sure I had moments where I’d forget things or get scattered, but it wasn’t standing out to me in the same way. Once he came to stay with us and there were more things to keep track of, more responsibility in the house, that’s when I really started noticing that I wasn’t keeping up as well as I thought I should.

So I guess the timing does line up with that period. I wouldn’t want to say the surgery or him moving in “caused” it, because I don’t really know that, but that’s when it became harder to ignore.
